anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them, enlarging the version store and bloating tables and indexes.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Total in-engine memory demanded by caches, work areas, and background components pushes the host into sustained pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages and latches, creating wait spikes and CPU spin without corresponding throughput gains.

Combined anomalous phenomena: While the version store and heap bloat grow, ever-increasing dirty pages and old row versions must be kept in memory. This expands the buffer pool footprint and forces the engine to reserve more private and shared work memory, driving the overall RSS upward. Under pressure, the operating system begins paging; page faults slow down cleanup workers, which in turn fall further behind, allowing even more dead tuples to accumulate. Hot pages such as index roots, free-space-map pages, and version-chain heads become latch hotspots because both foreground queries (doing long MVCC visibility scans) and background cleaners (doing deletes and vacuum-style work) continuously touch them. Users observe a mix of high buffer-busy/latch waits, rising memory usage, erratic cache-hit ratios, longer table scans, frequent checkpoints, and occasional OOM terminations or instance restarts that are hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causal chain and reinforcement: Heavy update/delete churn produces large numbers of dead tuples, inflating both the heap and the version store. The extra pages must be cached and flushed, directly increasing memory consumption; when memory caps are exceeded, the OS pages out, lengthening I/O latency. Slower I/O prolongs latch hold times on dirty or hot pages, amplifying buffer contention. At the same time, memory pressure throttles or starves background cleaners, so version buildup accelerates, creating a feedback loop: more dead tuples ⇒ larger memory footprint ⇒ higher paging and slower cleaners ⇒ still more dead tuples. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another in a vicious cycle that degrades OLTP throughput and latency far more severely than any of them would in isolation.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
